# Tell the build what your system creates

<!-- type: tutorial · level: 2 · topic: contract -->

**Needs first:** [Parameters and launch files](parameters-and-launch-files.md)

<!-- BEGIN GENERATED by scripts/gen-board-support.py: chapter status -->
> **Status:** this chapter runs on [`nros-board-mps2-an385`](../reference/boards/mps2-an385.md): Verified in emulator (daily). From the board support registry; [Board Support Levels](../reference/board-support-levels.md) explains the words.
<!-- END GENERATED chapter status -->

Every node in the project creates publishers, subscriptions, timers, servers
and clients when it starts. On a board with no heap, the memory for all of
them is set aside when the image is built, so the build must size it before
any node has run. Until now it has not known what the nodes create, so it
sized every pool for a generous default. In this chapter you write the
**contract**: a file beside the launch file that states what the system
creates. You measure the image's static RAM before and after, and watch it
fall by more than a third:

```text
   text    data     bss     dec     hex filename
1132064    6288  613540 1751892  1abb54 .../baremetal_entry      (before)
1131656    4656  384484 1520796  17349c .../baremetal_entry      (after)
```

Then you break the contract on purpose and read the refusal, which shows
what the build does when a statement and the system disagree.

Run every step from the root of `sensor_ws`.

## Measure the image as it is

`nros build` prints the path of the image it built, after `artifact:`. Read
the image's sizes with the `size` tool of the Arm toolchain `nros setup`
installed:

```bash probe=810 track=installed variant=qemu
elf="$(nros build 2>&1 | sed -n 's/^  artifact: //p')"
"$(nros locate tool arm-none-eabi-gcc)/bin/arm-none-eabi-size" "$elf"
```

```text
   text    data     bss     dec     hex filename
1132064    6288  613540 1751892  1abb54 /home/you/sensor_ws/build/bare-metal-zenoh/baremetal_entry/target/thumbv7m-none-eabi/debug/baremetal_entry
```

Those are the numbers of a Rust project; a C or C++ project's differ, and
its image is under `build/` too. `text` is flash: the code and its constants.
`data` and `bss` are RAM that exists from the moment the board boots, `data`
with initial values and `bss` zeroed. This image claims 613,540 bytes of
zeroed RAM before its first instruction, which is what this chapter shrinks.
The build is a debug build, so `text` is large; `bss` is not affected by
optimization.

Where does it go? Each node's slots, the executor's storage for every
callback, the middleware's sessions and receive buffers, and a parameter
store, each sized for the most the system might create: up to 32 parameters,
four samples per subscription, and so on. The build warned about some of it
on every run, in lines like this one:

```text
warning: nros-rmw-zenoh@0.6.0: the parameter family's requests are not priced: the image declares no `params:`. Its inbox slot keeps 1024 B; a larger `set_parameters` is dropped with no reply. Declaring the parameters in the contract derives it (issue 1352)
```

## Write the contract

A contract is a YAML file with the launch file's name and `.contract.yaml`,
in the same directory. Write `launch/system.contract.yaml`:

```bash probe=820 track=installed variant=qemu
cat > src/sensor_node_bringup/launch/system.contract.yaml <<'EOF'
# What the system in system.launch.xml creates, so the build can size the
# image for exactly that. Names are the names the code and the launch file
# give: local endpoint names under nodes:, resolved names under topics:.
version: 1

nodes:
  sensor_node:
    params:
      period_ms: { type: integer }
    paths:
      on_tick:
        trigger: { timer: { rate_hz: 2 } }
        output: [reading]
    pub:
      reading: { qos: { depth: 1, durability: volatile } }
  monitor_node:
    params: {}
    sub:
      reading: { qos: { depth: 1, durability: volatile } }
  server_node:
    params: {}
    srv:
      add_two_ints: {}
  client_node:
    params: {}
    paths:
      issue_call:
        trigger: { timer: { rate_hz: 1 } }
        output: []
    cli:
      add_two_ints: {}
  action_server_node:
    params: {}
  action_client_node:
    params: {}

topics:
  /sensor/reading:
    type: tutorial_msgs/msg/Reading
    pub: [sensor_node/reading]
    sub: [monitor_node/reading]

services:
  /add_two_ints:
    type: example_interfaces/srv/AddTwoInts
    server: [server_node/add_two_ints]
    client: [client_node/add_two_ints]

actions:
  /fibonacci:
    type: example_interfaces/action/Fibonacci
    server: [action_server_node/fibonacci]
    client: [action_client_node/fibonacci]
EOF
```

Read it from the top:

- **`nodes:`** has one entry per node, under the name the launch file gives
  it. Under each, the endpoints the node creates are keyed by their LOCAL
  name: `reading`, not `/sensor/reading`. `pub:`, `sub:`, `srv:` and `cli:`
  are publishers, subscriptions, service servers and service clients.
- **`params:`** lists the parameters a node declares. The talker declares
  `period_ms`, the one chapter 7's launch file sets; every other node
  declares none, `params: {}`. That is not the same as leaving `params:`
  out, which says nothing.
- **`paths:`** is where timers live. A path with a `timer` trigger and no
  input is a periodic callback: the talker's `on_tick` at 2 Hz (the 500 ms
  of chapter 7) and the client's `issue_call` at 1 Hz.
- **`qos:`** states the quality of service an endpoint uses. `depth: 1`
  keeps one sample, and `durability: volatile` keeps none for late joiners.
- **`topics:`, `services:` and `actions:`** wire the endpoints together under
  their RESOLVED names, and carry their types. `/sensor/reading` is the name
  after chapter 7's remap, which is the name the board uses.

The build reads this file every time it builds the image, folds it into the
system it resolved from the launch file, and sizes every pool from it.
Nothing in a node package changes. The contract describes this launch file's
system, so a second launch file in the bringup gets its own contract, with
its own name before `.contract.yaml`.

## Mark the contract as unchecked

A contract is a statement beside the code, and the build can check it
against the code by building the same launch file for your host, running
that host program once in a recording mode, and comparing what the nodes
created with what the contract says. That check is the **census**. It needs
a host image of the same launch file in the bringup, and this one has only
the board's, so tell the build to warn rather than refuse when no census
exists:

```bash probe=825 track=installed variant=qemu
printf '\n[census]\non_missing = "warn"\n' >> src/sensor_node_bringup/system.toml
```

Every build of the image now says, in its output, that its pools come from a
contract nothing has compared with the code. Treat that line as a reminder:
the contract is yours to keep right until a census checks it.

## Measure it again

```bash probe=830 track=installed variant=qemu
elf="$(nros build 2>&1 | sed -n 's/^  artifact: //p')"
"$(nros locate tool arm-none-eabi-gcc)/bin/arm-none-eabi-size" "$elf"
```

```text
   text    data     bss     dec     hex filename
1131656    4656  384484 1520796  17349c /home/you/sensor_ws/build/bare-metal-zenoh/baremetal_entry/target/thumbv7m-none-eabi/debug/baremetal_entry
```

Static RAM fell from 613,540 to 384,484 bytes of `bss`, and `data` from
6,288 to 4,656: 230,688 bytes, 37 percent of the image's RAM, from a file of
about 50 lines. Most of it is the parameter store, now sized for the one parameter
the system declares instead of 32. The rest is the middleware's receive
buffers for one sample instead of four, and no retention for late joiners.

## Run it

The image runs as before, with less RAM:

```bash probe=840 probe-run=900 track=installed variant=qemu
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
nros run --expect 'I heard: reading 3'
```

```text probe-expect=840 variant=qemu
I heard: reading 3
```

The console says where the depth now comes from:

```text
[WARN] nros: [    0.089222] declared depth: taking KEEP_LAST(1) on publisher `/sensor/reading`; the call site asked 10 and the build reserved 1. Raise the contract row to keep more (type `tutorial_msgs::msg::dds_::Reading_`).
[INFO] sensor_node: [    0.100442] Publishing every 500 ms
```

The talker's code asks for a history of 10, the ROS 2 default; the image
reserved 1, because the contract says the system keeps 1, and the board takes
what was reserved. The talker publishes every 500 ms and the listener reads
each sample before the next arrives, so one is enough. A node that needs to
keep more says so in the contract, and the build reserves it.

## Break it on purpose

Rename the talker's parameter in the contract, from `period_ms` to `period`:

```bash probe=850 track=installed variant=qemu
sed -i 's#      period_ms: { type: integer }#      period: { type: integer }#' \
    src/sensor_node_bringup/launch/system.contract.yaml
```

and build:

```bash probe=855 track=installed variant=qemu
if nros build; then echo "the build accepted a contract that disagrees with the launch file" >&2; exit 1; fi
```

The build refuses, before it compiles anything:

```text
Error: 1 launch parameter value(s) disagree with the contract's declarations:
  node `/sensor_node`: parameter `period_ms`, set by launch file system.launch.xml, is not declared in its contract (/home/you/sensor_ws/src/sensor_node_bringup/launch/system.contract.yaml); it declares: period
```

The launch file sets `period_ms`, and the contract says the talker declares
only `period`. The build does not guess which one is right, and it does not
size the parameter store for the names that matched and ignore the rest. It
stops, naming the node, the parameter and both files. The model it resolved
is set aside as refused, so nothing builds from it until a resolve succeeds.

Put the name back, and the build succeeds again:

```bash probe=860 track=installed variant=qemu
sed -i 's#      period: { type: integer }#      period_ms: { type: integer }#' \
    src/sensor_node_bringup/launch/system.contract.yaml
nros build
```

## What just happened

You gave the build **the contract**, and it used it for **static sizing**:
every pool of the image sized from what the system states it creates, rather
than from a default large enough for any system.

A contract states, ahead of the build, what only exists after the program
runs. A node creates its publishers and timers in `register` or `configure`,
at boot, but the pools they live in are `static` arrays whose sizes are
compiled in before any node's code is. Somebody must state those numbers
before the build, and the contract is where the whole system states them
once, under the same names the launch file and the ROS 2 graph use.

Three rules make it safe to size from a statement:

- **Names are resolved names.** A contract row matches an endpoint, a
  parameter or a node by the name the system actually uses, after remaps and
  namespaces. A row that matches nothing is not used, and a value the launch
  file sets that the contract does not declare is refused, as you saw.
- **All or nothing, per image.** If one node of an image is missing from the
  contract, that image derives nothing and keeps its configured defaults. A
  count taken over only the nodes the contract describes would be smaller
  than the image needs, and a pool one slot short fails at boot, so the build
  refuses to guess "some of them".
- **Checked against the code when it can be.** The census compares the
  contract with what the nodes actually create. An endpoint the code creates
  and the contract omits is refused, because it is the pool that would be
  short; one the contract declares and the code never creates is refused
  too, unless the bringup waives it under `[census.waive]`. A census is
  fresh by content: touching a file changes nothing, adding a subscription
  does. This Tutorial's bringup has no host image to take a census with, so
  it warns instead; `[census] on_stale = "warn"` does the same for a census
  that no longer matches the code.

The same contract works for every language. A C or C++ node package has no
`ENTITY_BOUNDS`: its counts come only from the contract, which is why a
contract matters most for a C or C++ image. A bringup with no `launch/`
directory writes the same file as `system.contract.yaml` beside its
`system.toml`, and the build carries it to where the launch file is
generated.

[Static memory and pools](../background/static-memory-and-pools.md) explains
what each pool holds and why the sizes derived from messages are upper
bounds.

## Design background

The contract and the sizing it drives follow
[RFC-0124](https://github.com/NEWSLabNTU/nano-ros/blob/main/docs/design/0124-book-user-guide-organization.md)
D6 for this walkthrough; the census follows the contract's retirement of the
per-component `ENTITIES` list, which declared counts beside the code with
nothing comparing the two.
